title: Model Serving at Scale
description: Master request batching, GPU scheduling, model versioning, shadow mode comparison, A/B testing with statistical significance, and TensorFlow Serving vs Triton.

segments.text: Serving ML models at scale is fundamentally different from training. Training is batch — process large datasets over hours. Serving is real-time — process one request in ten milliseconds. Google serves over ten billion ML predictions per day across search, ads, and Gmail. The infrastructure for serving at this scale is as complex as the models themselves.

Request batching amortizes GPU overhead. Individual inference on a GPU wastes ninety percent of compute — the overhead of launching a kernel dominates. Batch eight to thirty-two requests together: GPU utilization jumps from ten percent to eighty percent. The tradeoff: batching adds latency while waiting to fill a batch. Use adaptive batching — batch up to sixteen requests or until five milliseconds, whichever comes first.

GPU scheduling for inference differs from training. Inference workloads are latency-sensitive — you can't queue for minutes. Multi-model serving on a single GPU uses time-slicing — model A uses the GPU for two milliseconds, model B for two milliseconds. NVIDIA's MPS allows spatial sharing — two models use different GPU cores simultaneously. Triton Inference Server supports both.

Model versioning tracks which model version serves which traffic. Deploy v2 alongside v1 — both loaded in memory. Route traffic: ninety percent to v1, ten percent to v2. If v2 metrics are better, promote to one hundred percent. If worse, rollback by routing everything back to v1. Keep at least two versions loaded for instant rollback.

Your recommendation model v2 increases click-through rate by two percent in A/B testing. But it also increases server latency from twenty to forty milliseconds. The product team wants it. The infrastructure team is concerned about doubling serving costs. How do you make this decision?
segments.thought_prompt: Model v2: +2% CTR but 2x latency and serving cost. How do you evaluate this tradeoff?

segments.text: Shadow mode deploys a new model alongside production without serving its predictions to users. Both models receive the same requests, both compute predictions, but only the production model's output is used. Compare predictions offline. This catches regressions — if the shadow model produces wildly different outputs, investigate before promoting it.

A/B testing models requires statistical rigor. Define a primary metric — click-through rate, conversion rate. Calculate the required sample size for your desired effect size and significance level. Netflix waits for ninety-five percent statistical significance before declaring a winner. P-hacking — checking results too early — leads to false conclusions. Pre-register your analysis plan.

TensorFlow Serving: production-grade serving for TensorFlow models. REST and gRPC APIs, batching, model versioning. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server: framework-agnostic — serves TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, and custom models. Supports dynamic batching, model ensembles, and multi-GPU. Triton is becoming the industry standard for multi-framework serving.

Model optimization for serving: quantization reduces precision from float32 to int8 — four times smaller, two to three times faster. Pruning removes near-zero weights. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher. ONNX Runtime optimizes computation graphs. These techniques can reduce serving costs by fifty to seventy-five percent with minimal accuracy loss.

Design the model serving infrastructure for a search engine serving one hundred thousand queries per second, each requiring three model inferences with sub-twenty-millisecond total latency. What's your GPU allocation, batching strategy, and failover plan?
segments.thought_prompt: Design model serving for 100K QPS, 3 models per query, sub-20ms total latency.

segments.text: Model serving at scale requires request batching for GPU efficiency, multi-model GPU scheduling, version management with instant rollback, shadow mode for safe validation, statistically rigorous A/B testing, and model optimization for cost reduction. The Staff-level principle: the serving infrastructure determines your model's real-world impact — a great model served poorly is a wasted model.
